description.narrative:
Oxfam proposes a ten months WASH project titled “Improving Access to Safe and Durable Water for Drought-Affected Rural Communities in Hargeisa” with a total budget of USD 787,000 under the SHF Reserve Allocation 2 (2025). The project aims to ensure equitable and durable access to safe water for 37,500 people (54 percent female; 42 percent children) across eight rural and 4 IDP hosting locations in Hargeisa District, with an additional 9,600 people reached indirectly. The action addresses recurrent drought and chronic water shortages in Somaliland’s dry rural belt, where water systems have degraded and communities rely on costly and unsafe sources. Thetarget locations and priority needs were identified through coordination with the Somaliland WASH Emergency Sub-Sector and a joint primary assessment conducted with the Ministry of Water Resources Development and local communities. The project will enhance water availability, quality, and system sustainability through climate-sensitive infrastructure, community capacity building, and inclusive participation of women and persons with disabilities. Key outputs and targets · 1 new borehole developed with solar pumping, 1 elevated tank, and 2 distribution kiosks serving 6,000 people. · 7 existing water systems rehabilitated and solarised in Bali Matan, Sabawanaag, Bender Wanaag, Cadaadley, Agabar, Salahley, and Darasalaam, providing improved water to 24,300 people. · 10 water filteration units (SkyHydrant or equivalent) installed to improve water quality at community and institutional levels. · 6 institutions (3 schools, 3 MCH centres) connected to piped safe water. · 1,200 households (7,200 people) supported through emergency water trucking or vouchers during critical dry spells. · 8 WASH committees (56 members) trained on operation and maintenance and equipped with toolkits for plumbing, electrical, and mechanical repairs. · 24 water quality tests, 32 hygiene promotion sessions, and 16 feedback sessions to strengthen safety, accountability, and behavioural change.
The project applies a safe programming approach in line with the Centrality of Protection Strategy and WASH Cluster guidance. A protection risk analysis will precede implementation, and all staff, suppliers, and community committees will receive orientation on PSEA and accountability. WASH committees will include at least 50 percent women and representation of minorities and persons with disabilities. Site designs integrate safety and accessibility featuressuch as lighting and ramps. A dedicated MEAL system will track results through baseline, endline, and continuous monitoring, measuring both quantitative progress (e.g. litres/person/day) and qualitative indicators (satisfaction, inclusion, functionality). Community participation and accountability are central. Local stakeholders will be involved in site selection, design, and monitoring. Responsive multi-channel accountability and and feedback mechanism (AFM) is established, including toll-free helplines and community sessions, tracked through a digital dashboards. The project promotes localization by engaging local technicians, suppliers, and water operators in all stages, coordinated with the Ministry of Water Resources Development, local authorities, and the WASH Cluster. The project will restore critical community water infrastructure, strengthen management capacities, and reinforce resilience to future droughts while ensuring safety, inclusion, and accountability for all groups in targeted locations in rural Hargeisa.
The proposed project directly aligns with the SHF RA 2 (2025) strategy for the drought response in northern parts, which prioritizes integrated, area-based interventions addressing acute water scarcity in severely affected rural Hargeisa. It contributes to the strategic objective of mitigating the impact of prolonged dry conditions by improving access to safe and durable water. Oxfam’s focus on developing new water sources, rehabilitating existing systems, and strengthening operation and maintenance responds to the WASH cluster priorities outlined in Section 5.1 of the Allocation Strategy. The project will also complements other SHF funded interventions in Hargeisa Rural supported under the same allocation ensuring geographic and sectoral coherence within the broader drought response framework.
By also integrating protection, gender, and disability inclusion, the project operationalizes the SHF’s Centrality of Protection guidance and Annex 1 requirements on safeguarding, accountability, and equitable access. The use of solar-powered technologies advances the allocation’s emphasis on environmentally responsible solutions, while engagement of local authorities, water committees, and private sector actors reinforces SHF’s localization and sustainability objectives. Overall, the project contributes directly to SHF’sintended outcomes of restoring essential services, reducing protection risks, and strengthening community resilience in drought-affected northern Somalia. IIndirect beneficiaries include community members and public service actors who will benefit from improved WASH service delivery and strengthened systems. Local leaders, water committee members, and operators will gain enhanced technical and operational capacity through training and engagement, contributing to better long-term management of water infrastructure. Households not directly targeted for water assistance will benefit from reduced pressure on limited water sources, safer water access points, and improved hygiene practices at community level through awareness and behavior change campaigns. Additionally, women, girls, and other vulnerable groups will indirectly benefit from reduced protection risks associated with long distances traveled to fetch water. The project will also strengthen coordination with local authorities, improving their ability to respond to water-related emergencies beyond the targeted villages.

participating-org.narrative: In 2004 Oxfam Novib set up a Liaison Office in Nairobi, Kenya in order to support the Strengthening Somali Civil Society Program, at the request of the EU. This request was based on Oxfam Novib's work in Somalia to date, but intended to be more widely directed atthe entire civil society sector and the specific context in which it is operating in a post-conflict country. The program started with consulting local organisations in Somalia and Somaliland to get a complete picture of the sectors and regions where they are active, the challenges they face and the relationship between civil society, local political structures and the private sector. A program was then developed to strengthen the institutional development of Oxfam Novib's partners and those of other Oxfams, as well as a range of new NGOs. In the first year local consultants were trained in Somalia. They were then seconded to civil society organisations to build their capacity in financial and organisational management. Furthermore, workshops were organised on specific themes suchas human rights and the role of civil society in the Somali context. The Liaison Office is now going to support the expansion of the program, focussing on strengthening both organisation and project management, while facilitating more training in the fields of civic education, governance, human rights and women's rights, HIV and AIDS and child protection. Over the years, the Somalia Country Office has expanded its intervention on short term humanitarian response as well as development development interventions. In 2015/2016, a decision was reached to move the Country Programme operation, which was largely in Nairobi, from Nairobi to Hargeisa. The country office has a small office in Nairobi , Kenya and large operations office in Hargeisa, Somaliland.
